description: The job is exception handling, not planning, and the system runs on relationships more than on software. Ask about the failure modes and the phone calls.

questions.text: How much of your job is executing the plan versus handling everything that breaks it?
questions.lands_because: Exception handling is the actual work, and framing it that way immediately separates you from interviewers who think supply chain is a spreadsheet.

questions.text: Where is the constraint in your network right now, and how did you know before the data showed it?
questions.lands_because: Constraint-spotting ahead of the reporting is exactly what expertise looks like in this field, and it is a satisfying thing for a practitioner to explain.
followups: Who told you? A person or a system?

questions.text: How much of this industry still runs on personal relationships and a phone call?
questions.lands_because: The persistence of relationship-based capacity brokering inside a supposedly digitized industry is one of the best untold stories in logistics.
followups: What can you get with a call that no platform will get you?

questions.text: Tell me about a shipment that went wrong in a way you had never seen before.
questions.lands_because: Logistics failures are concrete, geographically vivid, and often absurd. Reliable story generator with real systems insight underneath.

questions.text: What did the disruption years actually expose that was already fragile?
questions.lands_because: Reframes 2020-22 as revelation rather than cause, which is how people inside the industry think about it and how outsiders generally do not.
followups: Has any of it actually been fixed, or just re-priced?

questions.text: Who in this chain absorbs the cost when something goes wrong?
questions.lands_because: Follows the risk down the chain to drivers, small carriers, and warehouse labor. Structural framing makes it answerable without indicting anyone by name.
followups: Is that where it should sit?
